White & Bruce (1986) in Birds of Wallacea (BTO) stated that there was no justifiable reason to recognise Forbes & Robinson's sulaensis race, described in 1900, but this vocalisation suggests otherwise. rmk: This species is very unusual for a large pigeon since it seems to almost never call - I have never knowingly heard it. However, the wing noise it makes is distinctive and often leads to its discovery. Small numbers of this endemic subspecies can be seen around the top of Mt Sibela, occasionally down to at least 800m.

Low pigeon calls almost being drowned out by a cacophony of Buru Honeyeater vocalizations at dawn. Bird not seen, but Buru Mountain-Pigeons were common at this location with several birds doing display flights at dawn when this recording was made. Calls came from the general area where a number of pigeons were displaying. Over the course of six days at this site we encountered large numbers of mountain pigeons daily but never observed any other pigeons or fruit doves in this habitat. Despite being common and regularly displaying, the mountain pigeons were quiet and I only heard these calls on a few occasions right at dawn. The calls sound somewhat similar to those the Seram Mountain-Pigeon recording archived on xeno-canto. Given that the vocalizing bird was not seen in this case it is probably safest to consider this identification as 'probable' but given the location and circumstances I think it is very likely to be Buru Mountain-Pigeon. <https://ebird.org/checklist/S328271378>

file-name: XC116530-Possible scops on Pantar loudened_05 Sept 2009.mp3
rmk:
This mystery recording is from a mature mangrove woodland (approximately at S 8°23'20.95" // E 124°06'38.94").  It sounds like a Scops-owl to me but I failed to see it. The forest area was almost impossible to access (mangroves) adjacent to eucalypt woodland and I had no luck with playback. The calls sound however different then Otus magics tempestatis which occurs on nearby Flores and Lembata (Lomblen). But no Scops-owl is known from Pantar island, only a Ninox (Ninox [novaeseelandiae] plesseni is present (unlike Flores and Lembata where there is no Ninox).   I heard these calls from more then one location and on subsequent nights.  Peter Collaerts and friends also went to the same location and heard the same calls many months later (but also failed to locate and visually observe it - so a challenge remains...).

I had posted this recording earlier on Xeno-Canto but it has gone missing when Xeno-Canto transferred to the new server.  All comments / thoughts remain wellcome.  Anyone wishing to visit Pantar to check out these calls can contact me !

Two birds in the mangrove (at a 10-some meter) calling (to each other) at night:
the frequencies of the call are between 400 - 1400 Hz (comprising two simultaneous notes: between 400 - 750 Hz and 800 - 1400 Hz).

ID is supposedly Black Bittern based on experts' opinions, including XC202694.

Part one of twenty two minutes of recording I made of this bird circling two cornfields. It began at three thirty am when it was close to the lodge and it's call woke me thinking someone had been killed outside my door. Once I realized it was an owl I spent the next 40 minutes (with several pauses) with mic in hand listening as this bird circled over a far corn field before coming back and circling the closest field to me where it vocalized several times. The bird was only seen in silhouette against some faint moonlight. I kept much of the first five minutes of this recording whole to preserve the intervals in between calls. I did edit out some cracks and pops to clean it up a bit. This is the same bird in XC152131 and XC152132, which is the best recording as the bird was closest then. At four ten am it stopped calling and we tried some playback but it never returned.

A mysterious call recorded in hilly secondary forest with clearings -- well after dark (heard a few times with long intervals, making recording the sound a bit difficult).  Does this sound like a(n) (scops) owl to people ? No Scops owl is known from the Togian islands but the possible presence is mentioned in Forktail 22 (2006) - The birds of the Togian Islands, Central Sulawesi, Indonesia by Mochamad Indrawan et all:

[SCOPS OWL Otus sp.
Local people reported a small owl with ear-tufts from Benteng,Togian island, which clearly suggests a scops owl. Based on numerous local interviews this bird appears to be be more localised, if not scarcer, than Ochre-bellied Hawk Owl Ninox ochracea and Togian Hawk Owl N. burhani. The presence of a scops owl on Togian could have been predicted, and it may well prove to be a new
species. Sound recordings, photographs and specimens will be needed to investigate this.]

rmk:
The recording location gave question whether it was xanthonotus or consobrinus, since some Sabah species are known to extend down the eastern coast of Kalimantan. However, upon close examination, the call is very similar to the end part of call in XC91176 which shows that the population here is indeed Dark-throated. This is also supported by photo evidence, which shows the male with sparser and shorter streaks on the underpart.

Thank you James Eaton for checking this recording and confirming the id.

file-name: XC413319-0921_053012 mp3 edited Trumpet  Manucode displaying and Raggiana x Greater  hybrid Yakiu.mp3
rmk:
(The coordinates for this recording are not accurately indicated  -  This recording was made at Yakiu, a settlement inside Wasur National Park, right at the PNG border).  

At this site, I photographed and sound recorded what appears to be a little known display behaviour of the Trumpet Manucode. 

The presumed male was calling and displaying at dawn from the top of dead branch while the presumed female was sometimes sitting 10 cm lower jumping up and down on the branches just below the presumed male.   When you hear the calls accelerate,  the bird is calling (singing) while it flies off the dead branch and "climbs" with flapping wing about ten metres high in the sky before it dives down with its wings closed and then returns to the same branch.  After a while the whole spectacular ceremony starts again...   (photographs were takento illustrate these presumably little known/documented display flights).

Both new New Guinean fieldguides (Pratt & Beehler + Phil Gregory) indicate that the Trumpet manucode  is in need of a taxonomic revision and that it is likely that several cryptic species are involved. There appear to be significant vocal and haitat differences (lowland as well as montane forms); with vocalisations (display song as well as contact calls) not well understood.

Saw a small phylloscopus warbler. The proportions seemed a bit off (chunkier and less lean) compared to the usual arctic warbler. Bird looked different to the other Arctic Warblers seen. Recorded audio and it matched with the two-note "V-shaped" call that is distinct to the species. Filtered to remove low noise (environmental) and normalized (-3dB) to highlight bird sound. Took photos of a bird which shows a strong wing bar and slight yellowish-green coloration on the supercilium as well as on the flanks and near the wings, will be uploading photos later if possible to fix the exposure (backlit). Habitat: wooded/forest area but highly degraded was seen scrounging for insects in tree canopy (higher up).

rmk:
This is a clip taken from an ambient recording made during a point count in Gunung Nyiut Nature Preserve in West Kalimantan, Indonesia. The mystery is the three-note repeated whistled phrase high-low-low. I saw the bird briefly in early morning light about three meters off the ground in the understory of primary hill rain forest. It had a slate grey back and white on its vent/lower belly. It was about robin-sized, with a very thrushy bill and fairly stocky body. The color pattern was very similar to Copsychus saularis pluto, but I can't remember whether it had a wing bar, and it seemed to have more white on its belly, though not as much as musicus. However, I recognize that given the habitat, it seems very unlikely to be a Magpie-robin. As I remember, it also gave some more varied calls, but this is what I found when I opened up the recording. I'd appreciate any advice!

An additional bit of sound from this bird is XC411533

rmk:
This is a cut from an ambient recording made during a point count conducted as part of a larger study in Cagar Alam Gunung Nyiut, West Kalimantan. The forest is selectively logged primary rainforest, the weather was sunny and clear. 

The mystery in question is the trogon-like descending piping in the background. To me, it resembles the beginning of Scarlet-rumped Trogon's song in pitch and pattern, but the middle and end follow a Cinnamon-rumped Trogon-like rhythm in that the notes remain well-spaced instead of speeding up. It also decreases in volume and fades away in a similar manner to Cinnamon-rumped Trogon's call.

During the point count, I heard this call several times, and it followed the same pattern. Perhaps it's mimicry? Anyone have any ideas?

Any advice would be deeply appreciated.
